title: Homeostasis and Coordination (Extended)
description: Supplement detail for IGCSE Biology 0610: synapse events and one-way transmission, the antagonistic iris muscles, accommodation, rods and cones, glucagon, negative feedback control of blood glucose, Type 1 diabetes, and temperature control through the skin.

notes.heading: The Synapse: the Four Events (14.1.8–10)
notes.body:
📌 The structures (14.1.8)
At a synapse, the first neurone ends in a swelling packed with **vesicles** containing **neurotransmitter molecules**. Between the two neurones is a tiny **synaptic gap**, and the membrane of the second neurone carries **receptor proteins**. (The Core definition — a synapse is a junction between two neurones — is in the coordination topic.)

🔑 The four events, in order (14.1.9)
1. An impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone → vesicles **release neurotransmitter molecules** into the gap.
2. The molecules **diffuse across the synaptic gap**.
3. They **bind to receptor proteins** on the second neurone.
4. Binding **stimulates a new impulse** in the second neurone.

🔑 Why transmission is one-way (14.1.10)
Only the first neurone holds the vesicles, and only the second neurone holds the receptor proteins — so the signal can only travel forwards. Synapses therefore **ensure impulses pass in one direction** along a pathway.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the impulse 'jumps' the gap or that electricity crosses it. The electrical impulse stops at the end of the neurone; the gap is crossed CHEMICALLY, by diffusion of neurotransmitter molecules.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Release → diffuse → bind → new impulse.
• Vesicles on one side, receptors on the other = one-way only.

notes.heading: The Pupil Reflex: Antagonistic Iris Muscles (14.2.5)
notes.body:
📌 The mechanism
The iris contains two sets of muscle working as an **antagonistic pair** — when one contracts, the other relaxes:
• **Circular muscles** — rings running around the pupil.
• **Radial muscles** — spokes radiating out from the pupil like wheel spokes.

🔑 Bright light → pupil constricts
**Circular muscles contract, radial muscles relax** → the pupil gets smaller → less light enters the eye.

🔑 Dim light → pupil dilates
**Radial muscles contract, circular muscles relax** → the pupil gets larger → more light enters the eye.

🔑 Why it is a reflex
Light receptors in the retina → sensory neurones → coordination in the brain → motor neurones to the iris muscles (the effectors). The response is automatic and rapid, and it protects the retina from damage by very bright light. The Core pupil reflex (light intensity vs pupil diameter) is in the coordination topic.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping the muscle pairs. Memory hook: to make the pupil SMALL in bright light, the CIRCLE closes in — circular muscles contract. Dim light must then be the radial pair.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Antagonistic = one contracts while the other relaxes.
• Bright: circular contract, radial relax → constriction.
• Dim: radial contract, circular relax → dilation.

notes.heading: Accommodation: Focusing Near and Distant Objects (14.2.6)
notes.body:
📌 The parts that do the focusing
• **Ciliary muscles** — a ring of muscle around the lens.
• **Suspensory ligaments** — connect the ciliary muscles to the edge of the lens.
• **Lens** — elastic; it changes shape to **refract** light by the right amount so a sharp image falls on the retina.

🔑 Viewing a NEAR object
Ciliary muscles **contract** → suspensory ligaments go **slack** → the elastic lens springs back **fatter (more rounded)** → light is **refracted more strongly** — needed because rays from a near object are still spreading out when they reach the eye.

🔑 Viewing a DISTANT object
Ciliary muscles **relax** → suspensory ligaments are pulled **tight** → the lens is stretched **thin** → light is **refracted less** — rays from a distant object arrive almost parallel.

💡 Worked Example
A 'describe accommodation' answer earns a mark per linked pair: muscle state → ligament tension → lens shape → amount of refraction. Write all four steps for near, and all four for distant.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'the lens contracts'. Muscles contract; the lens is elastic and changes shape passively — fatter when the ciliary muscles CONTRACT, thinner when they relax. That reversal is the most-lost mark in this topic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Near = ciliary contract → ligaments slack → fat lens → more refraction.
• Distant = ciliary relax → ligaments tight → thin lens → less refraction.

notes.heading: Rods, Cones and the Fovea (14.2.7–9)
notes.body:
📌 Two types of light receptor in the retina
• **Rods** — sensitive in **dim light**; they give **night vision** but do NOT detect colour (black-and-white vision).
• **Cones** — work in brighter light; there are **three types of cone**, each sensitive to a different colour of light, and together they give **colour vision**.

📌 Distribution across the retina
• The **fovea** is a small region in the centre of the retina, directly behind the pupil. It is packed almost entirely with **cones**, and its function is to give the **sharpest, most detailed colour vision** for whatever you look straight at.
• Rods are more common towards the **edges** of the retina — which is why a dim star is easier to see out of the corner of your eye than when you look straight at it.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming rods give colour vision, or that cones work best in the dark. It is the reverse: rods = dim light, no colour; cones (three types) = brighter light, colour, concentrated at the fovea.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Rods: dim-light (night) vision, no colour.
• Cones: three types, colour vision, packed into the fovea.
• Fovea = centre of the retina = sharpest vision.

notes.heading: Glucagon and Adrenaline: the Extra Hormones (14.3.5–6)
notes.body:
📌 Glucagon (14.3.5)
**Glucagon** is a second hormone secreted by the **pancreas**. Where insulin lowers the blood glucose concentration, glucagon RAISES it — the two work as an opposing pair (the full control loop is in the next note).

📌 Adrenaline's extra effects (14.3.6)
Beyond the Core fight-or-flight effects on breathing rate, heart rate and pupil diameter, adrenaline also:
• **increases the blood glucose concentration** — releasing extra glucose for respiration in the muscles, and
• **increases the heart rate** — delivering that glucose and oxygen faster.
The exam angle: adrenaline prepares the body for action by supplying MORE FUEL as well as speeding up its delivery.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Attributing glucagon to the liver or the adrenal glands. Both insulin AND glucagon are secreted by the pancreas; the liver is the organ that RESPONDS to them.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Glucagon: pancreas hormone that raises blood glucose.
• Adrenaline raises blood glucose AND heart rate.

notes.heading: Negative Feedback and Blood Glucose Control (14.4.3–5)
notes.body:
📌 Negative feedback (14.4.3)
A **negative feedback** system keeps a condition near a **set point**: a change AWAY from the set point triggers a response that REVERSES the change, bringing the condition back. Rise → response lowers it; fall → response raises it. That is how the internal environment stays constant. (The Core definitions of homeostasis and insulin are in the coordination topic.)

🔑 Blood glucose control by the liver (14.4.4)
• **Blood glucose rises above the set point** (after a meal) → the pancreas secretes **insulin** → the **liver** takes up glucose and converts it to **glycogen** for storage → blood glucose falls back.
• **Blood glucose falls below the set point** (fasting or exercise) → the pancreas secretes **glucagon** → the liver breaks glycogen down into glucose and releases it into the blood → blood glucose rises back.
Insulin and glucagon are antagonistic hormones, and the liver is the effector organ for both.

📌 Type 1 diabetes (14.4.5)
In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas no longer secretes enough insulin. Outline of treatment: regular **insulin injections** (or an insulin pump), with doses matched to meals and activity, plus regular monitoring of blood glucose concentration and care with diet.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'insulin converts glucose to glycogen' as if insulin were an enzyme acting in the blood. Insulin is the SIGNAL; the LIVER is the organ that takes up the glucose and stores it as glycogen.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Set point + reversing response = negative feedback.
• High glucose → insulin → liver stores glycogen; low glucose → glucagon → liver releases glucose.
• Type 1 diabetes: insulin injections plus glucose monitoring.

illustration.alt: A negative feedback loop for blood glucose: a rise triggers insulin from the pancreas so the liver stores glucose as glycogen; a fall triggers glucagon so the liver releases glucose from glycogen; both return the level to the set point.
illustration.caption: Negative feedback: any move away from the set point triggers the opposing hormone — insulin when glucose rises, glucagon when it falls — and the liver reverses the change.

notes.heading: Temperature Control and the Skin (14.4.6–8)
notes.body:
📌 Skin structures to identify (14.4.6)
On a skin section, be able to label: **hairs**, **hair erector muscles**, **sweat glands**, **receptors** (touch and temperature), **sensory neurones**, **blood vessels** and **fatty tissue**.

🔑 Keeping body temperature constant (14.4.7–8)
The **brain** monitors the temperature of the blood and coordinates the responses:
• **Insulation** — the fatty tissue under the skin reduces heat loss, and hairs stand up (hair erector muscles contract) to trap an insulating layer of air — important in furry mammals, though vestigial in us.
• **Too hot** → **sweating**: sweat glands release sweat, and its evaporation takes heat from the skin, cooling the body.
• **Too cold** → **shivering**: muscles contract rapidly and involuntarily; the respiration this involves releases heat, warming the body.
• **Vasodilation** (too hot) — the arterioles supplying the skin surface capillaries **widen**, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost to the air.
• **Vasoconstriction** (too cold) — those arterioles **narrow**, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'capillaries dilate' or 'blood vessels move closer to the surface'. It is the ARTERIOLES supplying the surface capillaries that widen or narrow; the vessels do not move. And sweat only cools you when it EVAPORATES — say so.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Label the seven skin structures.
• Hot: sweat + vasodilation. Cold: shivering + vasoconstriction + hairs raised + fatty insulation.
• The brain coordinates; negative feedback restores the set point.

flashcards.definition: Tiny sacs at the end of the first neurone that store neurotransmitter molecules and release them into the synaptic gap when an impulse arrives.
flashcards.example: Vesicles release neurotransmitter only from the first neurone — one reason synapses transmit one way.

flashcards.definition: The tiny gap between two neurones at a synapse, crossed by neurotransmitter molecules diffusing from the first neurone to receptor proteins on the second.
flashcards.example: The impulse crosses the synaptic gap chemically, by diffusion — not electrically.

flashcards.definition: Impulses cross a synapse in one direction only, because vesicles are found only on the first neurone and receptor proteins only on the second.
flashcards.example: In a reflex arc, synapses keep the impulse travelling receptor → effector, never backwards.

flashcards.definition: A pair of muscles where one contracts while the other relaxes: circular muscles constrict the pupil, radial muscles dilate it.
flashcards.example: In bright light the circular muscles contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil constricts.

flashcards.definition: Changing the shape of the lens — via the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments — to focus near or distant objects on the retina.
flashcards.example: For a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the ligaments go slack and the lens becomes fatter.

flashcards.definition: Retinal receptor cells that are sensitive in dim light, giving night vision without colour.
flashcards.example: Rods around the edge of the retina let you see a dim star from the corner of your eye.

flashcards.definition: Retinal receptor cells of three types, each sensitive to a different colour of light, together giving colour vision in brighter light.
flashcards.example: Cones are packed into the fovea, so colour and detail are sharpest where you look directly.

flashcards.definition: The small central region of the retina, packed with cones, responsible for the sharpest and most detailed vision.
flashcards.example: When you look straight at a word, its image falls on the fovea.

flashcards.definition: A hormone secreted by the pancreas that raises the blood glucose concentration — the liver breaks glycogen down into glucose in response.
flashcards.example: During a long run, glucagon release keeps blood glucose from falling too low.

flashcards.definition: A control system in which a change away from the set point triggers a response that reverses the change, restoring the set point.
flashcards.example: A rise in blood glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers blood glucose back to the set point.

flashcards.definition: Widening (dilation) or narrowing (constriction) of the arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries, increasing or decreasing heat loss.
flashcards.example: On a hot day, vasodilation sends more blood near the skin surface so more heat is lost.

flashcards.definition: Rapid, involuntary muscle contractions when the body is too cold; the respiration involved releases heat and warms the body.
flashcards.example: Shivering, vasoconstriction and raised hairs are the combined response to cold.

questions.stem: What do the vesicles at the end of a neurone contain?
choices: Neurotransmitter molecules
Red blood cells
Receptor proteins
Electrical impulses
questions.explanation: Vesicles store neurotransmitter molecules ready for release into the synaptic gap. Receptor proteins sit on the membrane of the NEXT neurone, and impulses are electrical events, not stored cargo.

questions.stem: Why can an impulse pass across a synapse in one direction only?
choices: The synaptic gap is too wide to cross twice
The first neurone electrically repels the second
Only the first neurone has vesicles of neurotransmitter, and only the second neurone has the receptor proteins
Neurones can only conduct impulses towards the brain
questions.explanation: One-way transmission comes from the asymmetric structure: release machinery (vesicles) on one side, detection machinery (receptor proteins) on the other. The gap cannot be crossed backwards because the second neurone has nothing to release.

questions.stem: Which receptor cells in the retina provide night vision?
choices: Cones
Rods
Hair cells
Guard cells
questions.explanation: Rods are sensitive in dim light and give black-and-white night vision. Cones need brighter light and give colour vision; guard cells belong in plant leaves.

questions.stem: In bright light, how do the iris muscles change the pupil?
choices: Radial muscles contract and circular muscles relax — the pupil constricts
Both muscle sets relax — the pupil stays the same size
Circular and radial muscles contract together — the pupil closes completely
Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax — the pupil constricts
questions.explanation: The iris muscles are antagonistic: in bright light the circular muscles contract while the radial muscles relax, shrinking the pupil. Contracting radial muscles instead pulls the pupil open (dilation, the dim-light response).

questions.stem: How does the eye focus on a near object?
choices: Ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments tighten and the lens becomes thin
The pupil constricts until the object looks sharp
The retina moves closer to the lens
Ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments go slack and the lens becomes fatter, refracting the light more strongly
questions.explanation: Near objects need strong refraction: ciliary muscles contract → suspensory ligaments slacken → the elastic lens springs into a fatter shape. The first option describes focusing on a DISTANT object — the classic reversal.

questions.stem: Which hormone, secreted by the pancreas, raises the blood glucose concentration?
choices: Insulin
Glucagon
Oestrogen
Testosterone
questions.explanation: Glucagon is the pancreas hormone that raises blood glucose, acting opposite to insulin. Oestrogen and testosterone come from the ovaries and testes and play no role in glucose control.

questions.stem: After a meal rich in carbohydrate, blood glucose rises. What happens next in a healthy person?
choices: The pancreas releases insulin; the liver takes up glucose and converts it to glycogen, so blood glucose falls
The pancreas releases glucagon; the liver releases more glucose into the blood
The kidneys filter out all the glucose into the urine
The adrenal glands release adrenaline to store the glucose
questions.explanation: A rise above the set point triggers insulin, and the liver responds by removing glucose and storing it as glycogen — blood glucose falls back. Glucagon is the response to a FALL, and healthy kidneys do not excrete glucose.

questions.stem: A toxin blocks the receptor proteins on the motor neurone side of a synapse. What happens when an impulse arrives at the end of the sensory neurone?
choices: The impulse jumps the gap electrically, as usual
The vesicles fail to form, so nothing is released
Neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across the gap, but it cannot bind, so no new impulse is stimulated in the motor neurone
The impulse is reflected backwards along the sensory neurone
questions.explanation: Release and diffusion happen at the FIRST neurone and are unaffected; it is the binding step that fails. With no binding, no new impulse is stimulated, so the reflex pathway stops at that synapse.

questions.stem: During a long run, blood glucose begins to fall. Describe the negative-feedback response.
choices: The pancreas secretes insulin, so the liver stores even more glucose
The pancreas secretes glucagon; the liver breaks glycogen down into glucose and releases it, returning blood glucose towards the set point
The muscles stop respiring so no more glucose is used
The brain stops monitoring blood glucose until the run ends
questions.explanation: Negative feedback reverses the change: a fall below the set point triggers glucagon, and the liver converts stored glycogen back to glucose and releases it. Insulin would drive glucose even lower — the opposite of what is needed.

questions.stem: Which set of responses keeps body temperature constant on a cold day?
choices: Sweating and vasodilation of the skin arterioles
Shivering and vasodilation of the skin arterioles
Sweating and relaxation of the hair erector muscles
Shivering, vasoconstriction of the arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries, and hairs raised by the erector muscles
questions.explanation: Cold responses all conserve or generate heat: shivering releases heat from respiration, vasoconstriction keeps blood (and heat) away from the surface, and raised hairs trap insulating air. Sweating and vasodilation are the HOT responses.

questions.stem: Sweating only cools the skin when the sweat evaporates. Why?
choices: Sweat is secreted at a lower temperature than the skin
Sweat glands absorb heat from the blood
Evaporation takes heat energy from the skin
Sweat washes warm air away from the body
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a cooling process: the water molecules that escape take heat energy with them, drawn from the skin. Sweat lying on the skin without evaporating removes no heat — which is why humid days feel so much hotter.

choices: A change away from the set point triggers a response that reverses the change, restoring the set point
A change away from the set point triggers a response that makes the change bigger
A system that switches off all hormone release
A response that can only happen once and then stops
questions.explanation: Negative feedback always opposes the change that triggered it — rise triggers a lowering response, fall triggers a raising response — holding the condition near its set point. Amplifying the change would be POSITIVE feedback.

questions.stem: Which skin structure provides most of the insulation that reduces heat loss?
choices: The sweat glands
The sensory neurones
The fatty tissue beneath the skin
The blood vessels of the dermis
questions.explanation: Fatty tissue under the skin is the insulating layer that slows heat loss. Sweat glands cool the body, blood vessels adjust heat loss by vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and neurones detect temperature rather than conserving heat.

choices: Regular insulin injections, with blood glucose monitoring and care with diet
Daily glucagon injections
A diet deliberately very high in sugar
A course of antibiotics
questions.explanation: In Type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes too little insulin, so treatment replaces it: insulin injections (or a pump) matched to meals and activity, with regular blood glucose monitoring. Glucagon would raise blood glucose further — the opposite of the need.

questions.stem: Why is vision sharpest when you look directly at an object?
choices: The pupil is at its smallest, which sharpens the image
The image falls on the fovea, a region of the retina packed with cones
The rods are concentrated in the centre of the retina
The lens is at its thinnest for direct vision
questions.explanation: Looking directly at something places its image on the fovea, the cone-packed central region that gives the most detailed colour vision. Rods dominate the retinal edges, which is why dim objects are easier to see out of the corner of your eye.
